# From Uniformity to a Target Distribution {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

- [Where do random variables come from?](#where-do-random-variables-come-from)
- [The quantile transform](#the-quantile-transform)

## Where do random variables come from? {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="61%"}
- Algorithms generate sequences—typically in $[0,1]$—designed to mimic IID
  uniform random variables
- Pseudorandom number generators are tested so that their output [looks IID
  random]{.alert} in many demanding ways
- Parallel computation requires special care: streams must not overlap or
  [acquire unintended dependence]{.alert}
- [RANDU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RANDU) is a classic warning: simple-looking output can conceal
  severe higher-dimensional structure
- Physical generators may supply genuine randomness, but do not by themselves
  guarantee IID samples from the desired distribution
:::

::: {.column width="5%"}
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
![](assets/images/random-variables-not-from-stork.png){fig-alt="A stork carrying a bag labeled random variable, crossed out with a large red X" style="width: 100%; clip-path: inset(7.9% 0 7.9% 0); margin: -7.9% 0;"}
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Uniform numbers are the raw material; a [transformation]{.alert} produces the
target distribution
:::

## The quantile transform {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

A sampling design supplies

$$
U_i\sim\Unif[0,1],\qquad i=0,1,\ldots
$$

The design may be IID, Latin hypercube, low discrepancy, or something else. For a target cumulative distribution function $F$, define

$$
Q(u):=\inf\{x\in\reals:F(x)\ge u\}
$$

Then $Q(u)\le x \iff u\le F(x)$

&nbsp;

For $X:=Q(U)$

$$
\Prob(X\le x)=\Prob\{Q(U)\le x\}
=\Prob\{U\le F(x)\}=F(x)
$$

Thus each $X_i:=Q(U_i)\sim F$

[IID inputs yield IID targets <br>Other designs (Latin hypercube, low discrepancy, ...) retain their dependence
structure]{.alert}

[Try the quantile-transform examples in the companion `GeneratingSamples`
notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/sampling/GeneratingSamples.ipynb)

## Binomial random numbers {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

Suppose $X\sim\Bin(3,0.6)$

::: {.binomial-transform-table}
| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| PMF $\varrho_X(x)$ | $0.4^3$<br>$=0.064$ | $3(0.6)(0.4^2)$<br>$=0.288$ | $3(0.6^2)(0.4)$<br>$=0.432$ | $0.6^3$<br>$=0.216$ |
| $x\in$ | $[0,1)$ | $[1,2)$ | $[2,3)$ | $[3,\infty)$ |
| CDF $F(x)$ | $0.064$ | $0.352$ | $0.784$ | $1$ |
| $u\in$ | $(0,0.064]$ | $(0.064,0.352]$ | $(0.352,0.784]$ | $(0.784,1]$ |
| Quantile $Q(u)$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
:::

E.g., $U_0=0.63$, $U_1=0.02$, and $U_2=0.47$ produce $X_0=2$, $X_1=0$, and $X_2=2$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>If $u=0.70$, what value does the inverse transform produce? What about $u=0.90$?</span>
:::

---

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "CDF and quantile function for a binomial distribution with three trials and success probability 0.6, showing right-continuous CDF steps and left-continuous quantile steps"
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: 94%

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

plt.rcParams["mathtext.fontset"] = "stix"

support = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3])
cdf = np.array([0.064, 0.352, 0.784, 1.0])
blue = "#1f5a91"

fig, (ax_cdf, ax_quantile) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8), constrained_layout=True
)

# Right-continuous CDF: [left endpoint, right endpoint)
cdf_left = np.array([-0.5, 0, 1, 2, 3])
cdf_right = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 3.5])
cdf_levels = np.array([0, *cdf])
for left, right, level in zip(cdf_left, cdf_right, cdf_levels):
    ax_cdf.hlines(level, left, right, color=blue, linewidth=3)
for x_value, lower, upper in zip(support, [0, *cdf[:-1]], cdf):
    ax_cdf.scatter(x_value, lower, s=70, facecolor="white", edgecolor=blue,
                   linewidth=2, zorder=5)
    ax_cdf.scatter(x_value, upper, s=65, color=blue, zorder=6)
ax_cdf.set(xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel=r"$F(x)$", xlim=(-0.5, 3.5),
           ylim=(-0.04, 1.04), xticks=support,
           title=r"CDF of $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,0.6)$")

# Left-continuous quantile: (left endpoint, right endpoint]
u_left = np.array([0, *cdf[:-1]])
u_right = cdf
for left, right, level in zip(u_left, u_right, support):
    ax_quantile.hlines(level, left, right, color=blue, linewidth=3)
    ax_quantile.scatter(left, level, s=70, facecolor="white", edgecolor=blue,
                        linewidth=2, zorder=5)
    ax_quantile.scatter(right, level, s=65, color=blue, zorder=6)
ax_quantile.set(xlabel=r"$u$", ylabel=r"$Q(u)$", xlim=(-0.02, 1.02),
                ylim=(-0.18, 3.18), yticks=support,
                title="Quantile function")

for ax in (ax_cdf, ax_quantile):
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=14)
    ax.xaxis.label.set_size(22)
    ax.yaxis.label.set_size(20)
    ax.title.set_size(18)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.18)

plt.show()
```

$F$ is [right-continuous]{.alert}; $Q$ is [left-continuous]{.alert}

## Zero-inflated exponential random numbers {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

### CDF

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
Let $X$ be nonnegative with

- Probability $p_0$ of being zero and
- Otherwise an
exponential distribution with rate (mean${}^{-1}$) $\lambda$

$$
\Prob(X=0)=p_0,
\qquad
X\mid X>0\sim\Exp(\lambda)
$$

Its CDF is

$$
F(x)=
\begin{cases}
0, & x<0,\\
p_0, & x=0,\\
p_0+(1-p_0)(1-\me^{-\lambda x}), & x>0
\end{cases}
$$
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
For the plot, $p_0=0.3$ and $\lambda=1$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "CDF of a zero-inflated exponential distribution, showing a jump of size p zero at x equals zero"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: 100%

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

plt.rcParams["mathtext.fontset"] = "stix"

p_0 = 0.3
rate = 1.0
x_negative = np.linspace(-1, 0, 150, endpoint=False)
x_positive = np.linspace(0, 5, 600)
cdf_positive = p_0 + (1 - p_0) * (1 - np.exp(-rate * x_positive))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.8), constrained_layout=True)
ax.plot(x_negative, np.zeros_like(x_negative), color="#1f5a91", linewidth=3)
ax.plot(x_positive, cdf_positive, color="#1f5a91", linewidth=3)
ax.scatter([0], [0], s=95, facecolor="white", edgecolor="#1f5a91",
           linewidth=2.2, zorder=5)
ax.scatter([0], [p_0], s=85, color="#1f5a91", zorder=6)
ax.axhline(p_0, color="#d59b2d", linewidth=1.8, linestyle="--", alpha=0.9)
ax.text(-0.92, p_0 + 0.035, r"$p_0$", color="#b27a13", fontsize=18,
        math_fontfamily="stix")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$x$", fontsize=22, math_fontfamily="stix")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$F(x)$", fontsize=20, math_fontfamily="stix")
ax.set_xlim(-1, 5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.04, 1.04)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=14)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(alpha=0.18)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

---

### Quantile

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
Inverting the CDF gives

$$
Q(u)=
\begin{cases}
0, & 0<u\le p_0,\\[0.4em]
-\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\log\!\left(\dfrac{1-u}{1-p_0}\right),
& p_0<u<1
\end{cases}
$$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Verify that $F\bigl(Q(u)\bigr)\ge u$ and identify where equality fails</span>
:::
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
For the plot, $p_0=0.3$ and $\lambda=1$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Quantile function of a zero-inflated exponential distribution, showing a flat segment from zero to p zero"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: 100%

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

plt.rcParams["mathtext.fontset"] = "stix"

p_0 = 0.3
rate = 1.0
u_flat = np.linspace(0.001, p_0, 250)
u_tail = np.linspace(p_0, 0.995, 600)
quantile_tail = -np.log((1 - u_tail) / (1 - p_0)) / rate

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.8), constrained_layout=True)
ax.plot(u_flat, np.zeros_like(u_flat), color="#1f5a91", linewidth=3)
ax.plot(u_tail, quantile_tail, color="#1f5a91", linewidth=3)
ax.axvline(p_0, color="#d59b2d", linewidth=1.8, linestyle="--", alpha=0.9)
ax.scatter([p_0], [0], s=85, color="#1f5a91", zorder=5)
ax.text(p_0 + 0.025, 4.5, r"$p_0$", color="#b27a13", fontsize=18,
        math_fontfamily="stix")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$u$", fontsize=22, math_fontfamily="stix")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$Q(u)$", fontsize=20, math_fontfamily="stix")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 5.2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=14)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(alpha=0.18)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

## Gaussian mixture random numbers {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

Let the one-dimensional target be a [Gaussian mixture]{.alert}:

$$
X\sim p\Norm(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)+(1-p)\Norm(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2),
\qquad 0<p<1
$$

Writing $\phi$ and $\Phi$ for the standard normal PDF and CDF,

\begin{align*}
\varrho_X(x)
&=\frac{p}{\sigma_1}\phi\!\left(\frac{x-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\right)
 +\frac{1-p}{\sigma_2}\phi\!\left(\frac{x-\mu_2}{\sigma_2}\right),\\
F_X(x)
&=p\Phi\!\left(\frac{x-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\right)
 +(1-p)\Phi\!\left(\frac{x-\mu_2}{\sigma_2}\right)
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
The PDF and CDF have analytic formulas, but the mixture quantile
$Q=F_X^{-1}$ generally has [no analytic closed form]{.alert}
:::

---

### Sampling without the mixture quantile

Numerically inverting $F_X$ would work, but a hierarchical construction avoids
solving $F_X(x)=u$

Generate $U_1,U_2\ \sim\ \Unif(0,1)$ and define

$$
C=\begin{cases}1,&U_1\le p,\\2,&U_1>p,\end{cases}
\qquad
X=\mu_C+\sigma_C\Phi^{-1}(U_2)
$$

Then $\Prob(C=1)=p$ and $X\mid C=k\sim\Norm(\mu_k,\sigma_k^2)$

::: {.key-point}
A mixture chains a [discrete component choice]{.alert} with a
[within-component transform]{.alert}
:::

---

### A concrete mixture

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
Take

\begin{align*}
p&=0.3,\\
(\mu_1,\sigma_1)&=(-2,0.5),\\
(\mu_2,\sigma_2)&=(1,1)
\end{align*}

For $U_1=0.24$ and $U_2=0.90$,

\begin{align*}
C&=1,\\
X&=-2+0.5\Phi^{-1}(0.90)\\
 &\approx -1.36
\end{align*}

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Use $U_1=0.70$ and $U_2=0.25$. Which component is selected, and what value of $X$ is generated?</span>
:::
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Density of a two-component Gaussian mixture with both weighted component densities shown"
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: 100%

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

plt.rcParams["mathtext.fontset"] = "stix"

p = 0.3
mu_1, sigma_1 = -2, 0.5
mu_2, sigma_2 = 1, 1
x = np.linspace(-4.5, 4.5, 700)

weighted_density_1 = p * norm.pdf(x, loc=mu_1, scale=sigma_1)
weighted_density_2 = (1 - p) * norm.pdf(x, loc=mu_2, scale=sigma_2)
mixture_density = weighted_density_1 + weighted_density_2

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.8), constrained_layout=True)
ax.plot(x, mixture_density, color="#1f5a91", linewidth=3.2,
        label=r"$\varrho_X(x)$")
ax.plot(x, weighted_density_1, color="#d59b2d", linewidth=2.2,
        linestyle="--", label=r"$p\,\varrho_1(x)$")
ax.plot(x, weighted_density_2, color="#4f9b8f", linewidth=2.2,
        linestyle="--", label=r"$(1-p)\,\varrho_2(x)$")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$x$", fontsize=22, math_fontfamily="stix")
ax.set_ylabel("density", fontsize=18)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=14)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(alpha=0.18)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=15)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

## Independent marginals {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

For $\vX=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ with [independent marginals]{.alert}

$$
\vX=\bigl(Q_1(U_1),\ldots,Q_d(U_d)\bigr),
\qquad
\vU\sim\Unif[0,1]^d
$$

where $Q_j$ is the quantile function of $X_j$

Store $n$ sampled vectors as an $n\times d$ array:

$$
\mX=
\begin{pmatrix}
X_{11} & X_{12} & \cdots & X_{1d}\\
\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots\\
X_{n1} & X_{n2} & \cdots & X_{nd}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

[Rows are samples<br>Columns are coordinates]{.alert}

## Multivariate normal sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

Let $\vZ\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mI_d)$ be a column vector of $d$ independent
standard normal random variables, so

$$
\Ex(\vZ)=\vzero,
\qquad
\Ex(\vZ\vZ^\mathsf{T})=\mI_d
$$

Define $\vX=\mA\vZ+\vmu$. Then

\begin{align*}
\Ex(\vX) &= \vmu,\\
\cov(\vX) &= \Ex\bigl[(\vX-\vmu)(\vX-\vmu)^\mathsf{T}\bigr]
 =\Ex(\mA\vZ\vZ^\mathsf{T}\mA^\mathsf{T})\\
 &=\mA\Ex(\vZ\vZ^\mathsf{T})\mA^\mathsf{T}
 =\mA\mA^\mathsf{T}
\end{align*}

Every [linear combination]{.alert} of the components of $\vX$ is normal; thus,
if $\mSigma=\mA\mA^\mathsf{T}$,

$$
\vX=\mA\vZ+\vmu\sim\Norm(\vmu,\mSigma)
$$

## Cholesky factorization {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

### Concrete example

For symmetric positive-definite $\mSigma$, Cholesky factorization gives a
[lower-triangular]{.alert} $\mA$ such that $\mSigma=\mA\mA^\mathsf{T}$

For

$$
\mSigma=\begin{pmatrix}3&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mA=\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&0\\a_{21}&a_{22}\end{pmatrix}
$$

matching the entries of $\mSigma=\mA\mA^\mathsf{T}$ gives

\begin{align*}
a_{11}^2&=3,
&a_{11}a_{21}&=-1,
&a_{21}^2+a_{22}^2&=1
\end{align*}

Hence

$$
a_{11}=\sqrt3,
\qquad a_{21}=-\frac1{\sqrt3},
\qquad a_{22}=\sqrt{\frac23},
\qquad
\mA_{\mathrm{Chol}}
=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt3&0\\-1/\sqrt3&\sqrt{2/3}\end{pmatrix}
$$

---

### General $2\times2$ covariance

For

$$
\mSigma=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_1^2 & \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2\\
\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 & \sigma_2^2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mA=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_1 & 0\\
\rho\sigma_2 & \sigma_2\sqrt{1-\rho^2}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Different factorizations generate the [same distribution]{.alert} but may behave
[differently under low discrepancy sampling]{.alert}

## Principal-component (PCA) factorization {#principal-component-factorization .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

For the [same covariance matrix as in the Cholesky example](#cholesky-factorization),

$$
\mSigma=\begin{pmatrix}3&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},
$$

let $c=\cos(\mpi/8)$ and $s=\sin(\mpi/8)$. The ordered eigendecomposition is

$$
\mV=(\vv_1\ \vv_2)=
\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mLambda=\operatorname{diag}(2+\sqrt2,\,2-\sqrt2)
$$

The PCA factor simplifies to

$$
\mA_{\mathrm{PCA}}=\mV\mLambda^{1/2}
=\begin{pmatrix}
1+1/\sqrt2&1-1/\sqrt2\\
-1/\sqrt2&1/\sqrt2
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Thus
$\mA_{\mathrm{PCA}}\mA_{\mathrm{PCA}}^\mathsf{T}
=\mV\mLambda\mV^\mathsf{T}=\mSigma$, just as for the Cholesky factor

## Gaussian processes {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="probability"}

A Gaussian process is a random function whose values at [any finite collection
of inputs]{.alert} form a multivariate normal random vector

$$
g\sim\GP(\mu,K)
$$

means

\begin{align*}
\Ex[g(t)] &= \mu(t),\\
\Ex\bigl[\{g(t)-\mu(t)\}\{g(x)-\mu(x)\}\bigr] &= K(t,x)
\end{align*}

For inputs $t_1,\ldots,t_d$

$$
\bigl(g(t_1),\ldots,g(t_d)\bigr)^\mathsf{T}
\sim\Norm(\vmu,\mSigma),
\qquad
\Sigma_{jk}=K(t_j,t_k)
$$

## Brownian motion {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="probability"}

### Definition

Brownian motion $B$ is the Gaussian process with

$$
\mu(t)=0,
\qquad
K(t,x)=\min(t,x),
\qquad t,x\ge0
$$

For $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_d$

$$
\bigl(B(t_1),\ldots,B(t_d)\bigr)^\mathsf{T}
\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mSigma),
\qquad
\Sigma_{jk}=\min(t_j,t_k)
$$

The covariance structure implies [independent normal increments]{.alert}

---

### Covariance matrix and Cholesky factor

For $0<t_1<t_2<t_3$, let $\Delta t_1=t_1$ and
$\Delta t_j=t_j-t_{j-1}$. Then

$$
\mSigma=
\begin{pmatrix}
t_1&t_1&t_1\\
t_1&t_2&t_2\\
t_1&t_2&t_3
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mA=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sqrt{\Delta t_1}&0&0\\
\sqrt{\Delta t_1}&\sqrt{\Delta t_2}&0\\
\sqrt{\Delta t_1}&\sqrt{\Delta t_2}&\sqrt{\Delta t_3}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mSigma=\mA\mA^\mathsf{T}
$$

[Each entry sums the increments shared by both times]{.alert}:

$$
(\mA\mA^\mathsf{T})_{jk}
=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\min(j,k)}\Delta t_\ell
=t_{\min(j,k)}
$$

In general, $A_{jk}=\sqrt{\Delta t_k}$ for $k\le j$ and $A_{jk}=0$ otherwise

---

### Sampling

Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_d\ \IIDsim\ \Norm(0,1)$ and start from $B(t_0)=0$

$$
B(t_j)=B(t_{j-1})+\sqrt{t_j-t_{j-1}}\,Z_j,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,d
$$

Equivalently

$$
B(t_j)=\sum_{k=1}^j\sqrt{t_k-t_{k-1}}\,Z_k
$$

::: {.key-point}
The Cholesky construction is the familiar [cumulative-sum construction]{.alert} for Brownian motion
:::

## Geometric Brownian motion {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="probability"}

For $S_0>0$, drift $\gamma$, and volatility $\sigma>0$, define

$$
S(t)=S_0\exp\!\left[
\left(\gamma-\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)t+\sigma B(t)
\right]
$$

Then $S(t)>0$ and its multiplicative increments are lognormal

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Using $B(t)\sim\Norm(0,t)$ and the normal moment-generating function,
show that $\Ex[S(t)]=S_0\me^{\gamma t}$. Hence determine $\gamma$ so that
$\Ex[S(t)]=S_0\me^{rt}$.</span>
:::

The correction [$-\sigma^2/2$]{.alert} makes $\gamma$ the mean growth rate;
the median growth rate is $\gamma-\sigma^2/2$

---

### Why the mean exceeds the median

Let

$$
m(t)=S_0\me^{(\gamma-\sigma^2/2)t},
$$

the median of $S(t)$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>The normal density weights the shocks $b$ and $-b$ equally. Show that
$$
\frac{m(t)\me^{\sigma b}+m(t)\me^{-\sigma b}}{2}
=m(t)\cosh(\sigma b)>m(t),\qquad b\ne0.
$$
Why do equal and opposite log shocks not cancel in price?</span>
:::

---

### Risk-neutral asset-price paths

For a non-dividend-paying asset with continuously compounded risk-free rate
$r$, the [risk-neutral model]{.alert} sets $\gamma=r$

On $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_d=T$, define $\Delta t_j:=t_j-t_{j-1}$. For
$Z_1,\ldots,Z_d\ \IIDsim\ \Norm(0,1)$,

$$
S_j=S_{j-1}\exp\!\left[
\left(r-\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)\Delta t_j
+\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t_j}\,Z_j
\right],
\qquad j=1,\ldots,d
$$

For equally spaced monitoring times, $\Delta t_j=T/d$

The simulated vector $(S_1,\ldots,S_d)$ is the [discrete asset path]{.alert}
used to evaluate option payoffs

## Option payoffs and prices {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="quant-finance"}

The fair price is the [expected discounted payoff]{.alert}

$$
\mu=\Ex(\text{discounted payoff})
$$

\begin{align*}
K &= \text{the }\alert{\text{strike price}},
& T &= \text{the }\alert{\text{time to maturity}},\\
t_j &= jT/d,
& S_j &= S(t_j), \qquad j=0,\ldots,d
\end{align*}

::: {.option-payoff-table}
| Contract | Discounted payoff |
|:---|:---|
| [European]{.alert} call | $\me^{-rT}\max\{S_d-K,0\}$ |
| [European]{.alert} put | $\me^{-rT}\max\{K-S_d,0\}$ |
| [Arithmetic Asian]{.alert} call | $\displaystyle \me^{-rT}\max\left\{\frac1T\int_0^T S(t)\,\dif t-K,0\right\}\approx \me^{-rT}\max\{A_d-K,0\}$ |
:::

QMCPy `FinancialOption` offers the [right]{.alert} and
[trapezoidal]{.alert} rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_d^{\mathrm{right}}
&=\frac1d\sum_{j=1}^d S_j,
&
A_d^{\mathrm{trap}}
&=\frac1d\left(\frac{S_0}{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}S_j+\frac{S_d}{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

---

### Path-dependent contracts

Asian, lookback, and barrier payoffs depend on the monitored path, not only
the terminal price $S_d$

At the monitoring times define

$$
m_d:=\min_{0\le j\le d}S_j,
\qquad
M_d:=\max_{0\le j\le d}S_j
$$

For a barrier $B$, let $\mathcal A_B$ be the event that the discretely
monitored path activates the option

QMCPy takes $S_0<B$ for an [up]{.alert} barrier and $S_0>B$ for a
[down]{.alert} barrier

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{up-in}: \mathcal A_B=\{M_d\ge B\},
& \text{up-out}: \mathcal A_B=\{M_d<B\},\\
\text{down-in}: \mathcal A_B=\{m_d\le B\},
& \text{down-out}: \mathcal A_B=\{m_d>B\}
\end{array}
$$

---

### Lookback and barrier payoffs

Using $m_d$, $M_d$, and $\mathcal A_B$ from the preceding slide:

::: {.option-payoff-table}
| Contract | Discounted payoff |
|:---|:---|
| [Lookback]{.alert} call | $\me^{-rT}(S_d-m_d)$ |
| [Lookback]{.alert} put | $\me^{-rT}(M_d-S_d)$ |
| [Barrier]{.alert} call | $\me^{-rT}\max\{S_d-K,0\}\indic(\mathcal A_B)$ |
| [Barrier]{.alert} put | $\me^{-rT}\max\{K-S_d,0\}\indic(\mathcal A_B)$ |
:::

---

### American put: optimal stopping

At the exercise times $t_0,\ldots,t_d$, the holder chooses a stopping index
$J$ using only prices observed through $t_J$

Let $\mathcal T_d$ be the set of these stopping indices. The fair price is

$$
\mu_{\mathrm{AmPut}}
=\sup_{J\in\mathcal T_d}
\Ex\!\left[
\me^{-rt_J}\max\{K-S_J,0\}
\right]
$$

- A [European put]{.alert} restricts exercise to $J=d$
- An [American put]{.alert} may exercise earlier when doing so is more valuable
- With no dividends and $r\ge0$, early exercise does not improve an American
  call, so we omit it here

# Low Discrepancy Sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

- [What does low discrepancy mean?](#what-does-low-discrepancy-mean)
- [Low discrepancy sequences](#low-discrepancy-sequences)
- [Why coordinate order matters](#why-coordinate-order-matters)

## What does low discrepancy mean? {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

Relaxing the requirement that $\vU_0,\ldots,\vU_{n-1}$ be IID allows carefully
constructed samples to cover $[0,1]^d$ more evenly

$$
\vU_0,\ldots,\vU_{n-1}\ \LDsim\ \Unif[0,1]^d
$$

The empirical distribution of the sample is close to the uniform distribution

[Discrepancy]{.alert} quantifies that difference; precise definitions come later

::: {.key-point}
Low discrepancy replaces independent placement by [deliberate coverage]{.alert}
:::

## Low discrepancy sequences {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

Important families include

- digital sequences, especially Sobol' sequences
- lattice sequences
- Halton sequences
- Kronecker sequences

They are available in deterministic and randomized forms through SciPy and
[QMCPy](https://qmcpy.org/)

In software arrays rows correspond to samples and columns to coordinates

## Why coordinate order matters {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

Return to the [PCA factorization](#principal-component-factorization):

$$
\vX-\vmu
=\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}\,\vv_1\Phi^{-1}(U_1)
+\sqrt{2-\sqrt2}\,\vv_2\Phi^{-1}(U_2)
$$

so $U_1$ drives
$\lambda_1/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)=(2+\sqrt2)/4\approx85.4\%$
of the total marginal variance

- [IID inputs]{.alert}: column order does not change the distribution
- [Low discrepancy inputs]{.alert}: column order changes which coordinate
  drives each principal direction

::: {.key-point}
Put the largest eigenvalues first so dominant directions use the low-numbered
coordinates, where many low discrepancy constructions are strongest
:::

# More Advanced Direct Sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

- [Transport maps](#transport-maps)
- [Acceptance–rejection sampling](#acceptancerejection-sampling)

[Transport maps and acceptance–rejection notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/sampling/TransportMapsAndAcceptanceRejection.ipynb)

## Transport maps {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

The quantile transform is a [one-dimensional transport]{.alert}

In $d$ dimensions

- Start with an easy [proposal]{.alert} density $\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$
- Seek the [target]{.alert} density $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$ through an
  invertible, differentiable map $T:\reals^d\to\reals^d$, where
  $\vZ\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ and $\vX=T(\vZ)$

The map transports the proposal to the target when
$\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\bigl(T(\vz)\bigr)
\left|\det\nabla T(\vz)\right|
=\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)$

Then, for every integrable function $f$,

\begin{align*}
\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(\vX)]
&=\Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}[f\bigl(T(\vZ)\bigr)]\\
&\approx \frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f\bigl(T(\vZ_i)\bigr),
\qquad
\vZ_0,\ldots,\vZ_{n-1}\ \IIDsim\ \varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
An exact transport [moves every proposal sample]{.alert} and makes the
correction weight equal to one
:::

[Normalizing flow]{.alert} builds a flexible transport by composing
manageable invertible maps, $T=T_m\circ\cdots\circ T_1$

---

### How is $T$ chosen?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
<h3>Mechanics</h3>

- Choose a tractable family $T_\theta$: affine, triangular, or a composition
  of simple invertible maps
- Determine $\theta$ analytically when possible; otherwise fit it so the
  density-matching equation holds approximately
- Add an optimality criterion when needed; quadratic-cost transport leads to
  a Monge--Ampère PDE
- Validate the transformed samples and the Jacobian calculation
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
<h3>The art</h3>

- In $d>1$, the proposal and target densities do [not identify a unique
  map]{.alert}
- Match the map family to the target's support, dependence, and geometry
- Choose coordinate ordering and the structure to preserve or simplify
- Balance accuracy against fitting, inversion, Jacobian, and sampling costs
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
The density equation supplies the constraint; the designer supplies the
structure that makes the map solvable and useful
:::

---

### A uniform proposal becomes a triangular target

Let the proposal and target densities be

$$
\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z)=1,\quad 0<z<1,
\qquad
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)=2x,\quad 0<x<1
$$

The target is $\operatorname{Beta}(2,1)$ with
$F_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)=x^2$, so its quantile transport is

$$
T(z)=F_{\mathrm{tar}}^{-1}(z)=\sqrt z,
\qquad
X=T(Z),\quad Z\sim\Unif(0,1)
$$

Indeed, for $0<z<1$,

$$
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\bigl(T(z)\bigr)T'(z)
=2\sqrt z\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt z}
=1
=\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z)
$$

Thus, for every integrable $f$,

$$
\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(X)]
=\Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}\!\left[f\bigl(\sqrt Z\bigr)\right]
$$

---

### A triangular flow creates curved dependence

Let $Z_1,Z_2\ \IIDsim\ \Norm(0,1)$ and, for $b>0$, define

$$
X_1=Z_1,
\qquad
X_2=Z_2+b(Z_1^2-1)
$$

This nonlinear map is easy to invert and has a simple Jacobian:

$$
T_b^{-1}(\vx)
=\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2-b(x_1^2-1)\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\nabla T_b(\vz)
=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2bz_1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det\nabla T_b=1
$$

Thus, with $\phi$ the standard normal density,

$$
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x_1,x_2)
=\phi(x_1)\phi\!\left(x_2-b(x_1^2-1)\right),
\qquad
\Ex(X_2\mid X_1=x_1)=b(x_1^2-1)
$$

- One flow layer: independent Gaussian coordinates $\longrightarrow$ curved,
  dependent target
- No useful map: [acceptance–rejection sampling]{.alert} as another direct
  route

## Acceptance–rejection sampling {#acceptancerejection-sampling .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

Ingredients

- [Proposal]{.alert}: sample $Z$ from known density
  $\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$
- [Possibly unnormalized target]{.alert}: known $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$;
  desired $X$ density $c\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$ for some $c>0$
- [Global envelope]{.alert}: known $M$ with
  $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)\le M\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(x)$ for all $x$

Sampler for $X_0,\ldots,X_{n-1}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
&i\leftarrow0\\[-0.2em]
&\texttt{repeat}\\[-0.2em]
&\qquad \texttt{repeat}\quad
  Z\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}},\quad U\sim\Unif[0,1]
  \quad\text{independently}\\[-0.2em]
&\qquad \texttt{until}\quad
  U\le\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(Z)}
  {M\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(Z)}\\[-0.2em]
&\qquad X_i\leftarrow Z,\quad i\leftarrow i+1\\[-0.2em]
&\texttt{until}\quad i=n
\end{aligned}
$$

[No normalizing constant $c$ needed]{.alert}

---

### Why acceptance–rejection works

[Acceptance indicator]{.alert}

$$
W:=
\begin{cases}
1, & U\le \varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(Z)/
           \bigl[M\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(Z)\bigr],\\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

[Density of an accepted proposal]{.alert}

\begin{align*}
\varrho_X(z)
&=\varrho_{Z\mid W}(z\mid1)\\
&=\frac{\Prob(W=1\mid Z=z)\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z)}
        {\Prob(W=1)}
&&\text{by Bayes' theorem}\\
&=\frac{\left(\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(z)/
        \bigl[M\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z)\bigr]\right)
        \varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z)}
        {\Prob(W=1)}
&&\text{by the acceptance rule}\\
&=\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(z)}{M\Prob(W=1)}
=c\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(z)
&&\text{since }c\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\text{ is a density}
\end{align*}

- [Acceptance probability]{.alert}:
  $\Prob(\text{acceptance})=\Prob(W=1)=1/(Mc)$
- [Expected proposal cost]{.alert}: $n(Mc)$ samples of $Z$ for $n$ samples of
  $X$

---

### The same target by acceptance–rejection

Uniform proposal and triangular target · [Notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/sampling/TransportMapsAndAcceptanceRejection.ipynb)

$$
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(z)}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z)}
=2z\le2
$$

- [Smallest envelope constant]{.alert}: $M=2$
- Generate independent $Z,U\sim\Unif(0,1)$
- Accept $X=Z$ when

$$
U\le
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(Z)}
{M\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(Z)}
=Z
$$

- [Acceptance probability]{.alert}: $\Prob(\text{accept})=\Ex(Z)=1/2$
- [Proposal cost]{.alert}: average $2n$ proposals for $n$ target samples
- [Exact transport]{.alert}: move every $Z$ to $\sqrt Z$
- [Acceptance–rejection]{.alert}: keep $Z$ with probability $Z$

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder" .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="prob-stat-est"}

- Start with uniform samples and transform them to the desired distribution
- The generalized inverse works for discrete and continuous distributions
- Mixtures combine a discrete component choice with a conditional transform
- Independent marginal transforms do not create dependence; correlated normal
  vectors require a matrix factorization, and PCA can concentrate variation in
  early coordinates for low discrepancy sampling
- Gaussian-process sampling reduces finite collections of function values to
  multivariate normal sampling
- Low discrepancy points trade independent placement for more even coverage
- An exact transport moves every proposal point to the target and makes the
  correction weight equal to one
- Acceptance–rejection samples from an unnormalized density when a suitable
  proposal envelope is available
